title: Statistics and probability for AI
description: Use summaries, denominators, and base rates to interpret results.
objectives: Use a base rate when interpreting a positive prediction
explanation: A mean sums values and divides by their count. A median describes the middle of sorted observations. Both summarize data, but a few extreme values can move the mean substantially. Always report the population, units, sample size, and missing-value treatment with a summary.

Probability describes uncertainty under stated assumptions. Conditional probability restricts attention to cases satisfying a condition. The chance a flagged item is truly positive depends on how common positives were before the test, as well as on the test errors. Sensitivity alone cannot answer that question.

Suppose 10 of 1,000 invented items are faulty. A detector catches 9 faulty items and falsely flags 99 good ones. Only 9 of 108 flags are real faults, about 8.3%. Check such counts before deciding whether a system can act automatically. A tiny evaluation sample also leaves substantial uncertainty about future performance.

terms.definition: Sum of observed values divided by their count.
The middle value, or average of the two middle values, after sorting.
How common an outcome is in the relevant population.

example: Four response times are 1, 1, 2, and 20 seconds. Their mean is 6 seconds and median is 1.5 seconds. Neither alone describes the slowest user experience, so also inspect the distribution and slow cases.
mistakes: Reporting a percentage without its denominator.
Assuming a small sample represents all users.
Confusing the chance of a flag given a fault with the chance of a fault given a flag.
exercise: Run summary_statistics.py. Replace the 20-second outlier with 2 seconds and predict the new mean and median. For the detector example, halve false positives and recompute the fraction of valid alerts.

code.title: Mean and median of response times

questions.question: Why can latency mean and median differ greatly?
questions.answer: A small number of slow responses can raise the mean while most responses remain fast.
questions.distractor: The median always includes only failed requests.

questions.question: What denominator gives precision for the detector example?
questions.answer: All flagged items: 9 true positives plus 99 false positives.

questions.question: Nine of 108 flags are real faults. What is the approximate precision?
questions.answer: 8.3%; most flags are false positives in this example.
questions.distractor: 90%, because nine of ten faults were detected.

questions.question: Why mention sample size with an accuracy estimate?
questions.answer: An estimate from few cases may be unstable and may miss important subgroups.
questions.distractor: Sample size makes every dataset representative.

questions.question: Should an unknown measurement automatically become zero?
questions.answer: No. Define and report a missing-data policy appropriate to what was measured.
questions.distractor: Yes, zero is always statistically neutral.
